name: Azelaic peel

card.summary: An azelaic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel (often around 20-30%) used in clinics to calm acne, reduce oiliness and even skin tone for clearer-looking skin.
card.note: Mild irritation and dryness possible; usually performed by professionals.

quick.overview:
Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used on skin for acne, rosacea and dark marks. In peel form it is applied in a clinic as a higher-strength superficial treatment, usually in a series of sessions.

The appearance payoff is fewer breakouts, less shine and a more even tone. In a study of 35 women with facial acne, a series of 30% azelaic peels was linked to lower sebum and fewer acne lesions.
quick.how: Peels are applied by a practitioner in a series, in the studies about every two weeks over several sessions, and are often paired with a home skin routine. Results build across the series.
quick.risks: Skin dryness and irritation are the main reported effects, and the studies described the peels as well tolerated. Not every study found a sebum reduction: in women aged 49 to 71, sebum rose after a 20% azelaic peel.

lead: An azelaic peel is a superficial chemical peel using azelaic acid, a compound that treats acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation in topical products.[3] Used as a peel, it is applied in a clinic in a course of sessions to reduce acne lesions, control oil and improve skin clarity.[1]

Azelaic acid has antibacterial activity against acne-associated bacteria, normalises follicle keratinisation, has anti-inflammatory effects and inhibits tyrosinase, lowering melanin production, which explains its use for dark marks and melasma.[3]
Published peel studies are small: one examined a 30% azelaic peel in 35 women with facial acne, and another compared azelaic and mandelic peels on sebum in ageing women.[1][2]

chain: Peel delivers azelaic acid to the skin surface
Acne bacteria, follicle blockage and melanin production are reduced
Fewer breakouts, less oil and more even tone
angle.text: The peel is used to reduce acne lesions and oiliness and, through tyrosinase inhibition, to even out dark marks. Its target is a clearer, more even complexion.

paras: Topical azelaic acid, typically at 15 to 20%, treats mild to moderate acne, rosacea, melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and is often suggested as an alternative to hydroquinone.[3] Peels apply a stronger concentration in a clinic setting for acne and oily skin.[1]
Mechanisms include antibacterial action against acne-associated bacteria without promoting resistance, normalising follicular keratinisation, anti-inflammatory effects and tyrosinase inhibition.[3]
Dryness and irritation are the main effects, especially in some people with eczema.[3] The 30% peel was well tolerated in the acne study.[1]

In a 2021 study, 35 women with facial acne received six 30% azelaic acid peels two weeks apart. Sebum secretion, lesion count and IGA severity fell significantly, and the procedure was well tolerated.[1] A 2013 study of 28 women aged 49 to 71 compared five peels with 20% azelaic or 40% mandelic acid and found increased sebum secretion in the U-zone, with no significant change in the T-zone.[2]
